name: ponyc
why: An actor-model language with reference capabilities for data-race freedom, a genuinely unusual design worth exploring.

brief.what_it_is: Pony is an open-source, object-oriented, actor-model programming language that compiles ahead-of-time to native code, with no interpreter or virtual machine. Its type system uses reference capabilities, labels on data that say how it may be shared, and the compiler checks those labels so concurrent programs can be free of data races without locks. The ponyc executable is the compiler; the Homebrew package also installs pony-agent-server, pony-dep, pony-doc, pony-lint, and pony-lsp. Programs can call C libraries through a foreign function interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Pony as a "get-stuff-done" language that puts correctness first, performance second, and simplicity third. It aims to make fast, safe, highly concurrent programs easy to write, with the compiler enforcing the guarantees instead of the programmer.
brief.how_it_works: Reference capabilities are labels attached to data types that describe how data can be shared: immutable data can be shared freely, and isolated data can only be exchanged. Actors are the unit of concurrency and communicate by asynchronous messages, with behaviours declared using "be" and called as methods on other actors. The compiler verifies these labels at compile time, which is how the project claims there are no data races, locks, or deadlocks.
brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: on Windows the minimum is Windows 11 or Windows Server 2022 (build 20348), and Windows 10 is unsupported. On Linux the minimum kernel is 5.3, because process support uses pidfd_open. Building from source needs an SSL/TLS development library (OpenSSL 1.1.x, 3.0.x, or 4.0.x, or LibreSSL) because the standard library's net package depends on it; CMake detects it and configure fails if none is found. The README points to INSTALL.md, BUILD.md (per-distribution package names), and INSTALL_DOCKER.md for further setup. I did not open those files. The brew caveats field is empty.
brief.standout: Most languages that prevent data races do it with locks, borrow checkers, or runtime checks. Pony instead puts reference capabilities in the type system so that the sharing rules are checked at compile time, and the README says it has no locks or atomic operations at all. Its homepage example of three actors coordinating a party is a short way to see the model.
brief.status: Maintained, but the evidence is limited. The README says Pony is still pre-1.0 with breaking changes arriving semi-regularly, and that applications are currently used in production. The README has a current platform support matrix and recent Windows and Linux minimums. I did not find a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so I could not confirm activity directly.
brief.caveats: Pre-1.0, so breaking changes happen semi-regularly. The homepage says the library ecosystem is small and there is no IDE. Windows 10 and Linux kernels older than 5.3 are unsupported. FreeBSD and OpenBSD are tested in CI but have no prebuilt binaries, and FreeBSD and OpenBSD arm64 are unsupported. Source builds need an SSL development library. The homepage explicitly says Pony is not the right choice today for projects that need a large ecosystem and stable APIs. The license is 2-Clause BSD.
quotes: Pony is still pre-1.0 and as such, semi-regularly introduces breaking changes.
Pony doesn't have locks or atomic operations. The type system ensures at compile time that your concurrent program can never have data races.
Share only immutable data. Exchange only isolated data. The compiler enforces both. No locks needed.
If you ask us, that's pretty damn cool.
